analysis.title: Impartial analysis of Measure Y

text: OFFICE OF THE CITY ATTORNEY One Twin Pines Lane, Suite 340 Belmont California BELMONT (650) 595-7414
Impartial Analysis Measure "Y" Belmont Community Center Measure

Measure "Y" asks Belmont voters whether to approve an ordinance levying a special tax for constructing and perating a new community center in the City of Belmont. Measure "Y" was placed on the ballot by a citizen initiative petition proposed by the group "Friends of Belmont Community Center" and signed by more than of 79/ registered Belmont voters. The measure requires a simple majority vote to pass.

If enacted, Measure "Y" would provide dedicated local revenue for the sole purpose of funding community center operations and services. To this end, the measure authorizes a tax on the square footage of improvements in the city beginning July 1, 2027, and establishes rates of 33C per square foot of improvements for dwelling units and 54C per square foot of improvements for all other property. The tax does not apply to parcels and improvements exempt from taxation by law and to the dwelling unit of persons age 65 and older who own and reside in the dwelling unit. Exemptions require annually eligibility verification.

The measure requires revenue from the tax be deposited into a "Community Center Special Fund" and restricts uses of that fund to construction, operations, staffing, maintenance, repair, and capital improvement of the new community center, administrative expenses associated with the tax, and for maintaining, improving, and expanding the community center's programs. Because the use of the revenue is restricted to these purposes, the tax is considered a special tax. The Community Center Special Fund would be controlled exclusively by the City of Belmont for those purposes and cannot be controlled or taken by the State.

The measure contains a list of spending priorities within the scope of the Special Community Center Fund to be considered by the City when spending the Fund. The priorities include certain types of capital, operational and programmatic expenditures related to the community center including: fire prevention, earthquake resistance, disaster relief, and other emergency preparedness; senior, adult, youth, and teen programs; supervised children's play, childcare and after-school programs; indoor and outdoor recreation areas; health, wellness, and fitness programs; improving accessibility and energy efficiency; and maintaining weekend and evening hours and appropriate staffing.

The measure is estimated to generate approximately $7.1 million for the Special Community Center Fund in the first tax year. The City Council may increase the tax rate by the percentage increase in specified regional inflationary or personal income growth indexes beginning in tax year 2028-2029. All other increases may only be authorized by the voters and the tax authorization would continue until ended by voters. The measure increases the City's appropriation limit under Article XIIIB of the California Constitution for four years by an amount equal to the revenue derived from the tax. The measure requires annual audits on the expenditure and administration of the tax.
California courts have held that a special tax measure proposed by citizen initiative requires only a simple majority vote to pass.
A "yes" vote would approve the measure and the levy.
A "no" vote would reject the measure.

A new recreation center is appealing, but /2 this FOREVER Tax is the wrong path. It asks residents to commit to a permanent tax without a clearly defined project or timeline. That's how good intentions lead to bad policy. 13 Your cost? At 33É/ft2, a typical 1,800 ft2 home will pay about $600 every year. A 2,200 ft2 home 2-0 will pay $726 yearly — FOREVER. Then rising with inflation! Landlords will pass the cost along to renters. Businesses, taxed at 54É/ft2, will have to cover costs too. Meanwhile, Belmont's Parks and Recreation budget expanded 46% from $7.6 million in FY 13 2021-2022 to $11.12 million today. This begs the question: is another tax really needed? For emergency facilities, Belmont already uses shared school district spaces throughout the city.. .without a permanent tax. Measure Y offers no concrete plan — and no end. Before we commit to a tax that never expires, we need to know what will be built, the cost, and a 2 ( completion date. We appreciate the range of ideas the City has explored. But ideas aren't the same as a defined / 3 project. A tax this gigantic needs a transparent plan with specific deliverables, costs. and timelines. Voting NO isn't rejecting a new community center.
